# Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction
Source: https://llmsx.org/tree/prodromal-pd-rbd-hyposmia-and-risk-prediction/

# Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction. Run status: COMPLETED.

<!-- generated by llms-concept-abstractor v1.5.1 · generated 2026-11-27 · budgeted to ≈8000 tokens; the full catalogue is llms-full.txt -->

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] A 2024 Mayo Clinic retrospective study matched 186 women and 186 men with iRBD; 48 patients (12.9%) phenoconverted during median follow-up of 6.0 years. Only age at diagnosis remained associated with conversion in the adjusted model (HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.06–1.13); the unadjusted association with antidepressant use must not be interpreted as evidence of neuroprotection. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11515114/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Isolated RBD involves dream enactment and loss of normal REM sleep atonia in the absence of an established neurodegenerative disorder. The cited risk cohorts used polysomnography-confirmed RBD; their estimates should not be assigned to questionnaire-positive dream enactment alone. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11515114/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11208573/
- [statement] Isolated RBD is a strong prodromal marker for a spectrum of neurodegenerative outcomes, including Parkinson’s disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy; a reported overall phenoconversion rate is therefore not a PD-only conversion rate. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11515114/
- [statement] A 2019 meta-analysis of seven prospective studies reported an association between hyposmia and subsequent PD, with pooled relative risk 3.84 (95% CI 2.12–6.95) across follow-up periods of 3–17 years. This relative risk is not an absolute probability that a person with hyposmia will develop PD. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6545790/
- [statement] RBD conversion estimates depend on population, age, endpoint definitions and ascertainment. The 2019 multicentre investigators warned that predictor hazard ratios should not be extrapolated to the general population, and the 2024 Mayo investigators called for population-based, polysomnography-confirmed cohorts to quantify community risk. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11515114/
- [statement] A negative baseline prodromal assessment cannot reliably rule out later phenoconversion in iRBD. In the 2019 cohort, even participants negative for the MDS prodromal criteria had conversion estimates of 5% at 3 years, 13% at 5 years and 27% at 8 years. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] The MDS research framework combines an age-based prior probability with marker likelihood ratios in a Bayesian naïve classifier; probable prodromal PD means at least 80% estimated certainty that prodromal disease is present, rather than an 80% prediction of clinical conversion within a specified number of years. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26474317/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11208573/
- [statement] Postuma and colleagues’ 2019 study followed 1280 polysomnography-confirmed iRBD patients from 24 centres: mean age was 66.3 years, 82.5% were men, and mean follow-up was 4.6 years. Overall conversion to an overt neurodegenerative syndrome was 6.3% per year, with Kaplan–Meier estimated conversion of 73.5% at 12 years; these are study estimates rather than universal individual prognoses. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/
- [statement] The 2024 Lifelines analysis found poor discrimination (ROC-AUC 0.577) using a subset of MDS risk and prodromal markers in 160 self-reported PD converters and 320 matched controls. Only six of eleven risk markers and six of twelve prodromal markers could be inferred, so this result scopes a partial, largely questionnaire-based implementation rather than invalidating the complete criteria. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11208573/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Prodromal PD describes early symptoms or signs of neurodegeneration before fully evolved motor parkinsonism permits a classic clinical diagnosis; the original MDS prodromal criteria were explicitly developed for research purposes only. (high confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26474317/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/
- [statement] In the same 2019 iRBD cohort, olfactory deficit predicted faster phenoconversion (adjusted hazard ratio 2.62), alongside quantitative motor abnormalities (3.16) and mild cognitive impairment (1.91–2.37); the outcome was overall neurodegenerative phenoconversion. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/
- [statement] Smell loss alone has limited specificity: it can occur in neurological diseases other than PD. The hyposmia meta-analysis explicitly cautioned that the limited evidence did not establish hyposmia as a solid stand-alone predictor of PD. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6545790/ · keywords: Prodromal PD: RBD, hyposmia and risk prediction · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6391615/
- [statement] The 2019 update of the MDS prodromal framework revised marker weights using new prospective evidence; in particular, the positive likelihood ratio for olfactory loss increased, while many marker likelihood ratios were unchanged. (low confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31412427/
